PROLOGUE
TO THE READER.

IT I S not possible to ob-
serve in everything one and the same
method and art in teach-
ing all languages, they be-
ing (as they are) so
distant and different from one another; rather,
uniformity in this would be a great de-
formity, and consequently confusion
and hindrance for whoever should learn them.
But with all that, it cannot be denied
that the plainest and shortest path
to make progress in any of the
languages is that which has been found for Latin
and Greek, as is seen by the artifice
with which they are taught and learned: both by
having reduced to a certain number al-

B l

Translation:

all the parts of speech, giving
them names according to their functions and qual-
ities, as well as for having shown
the variation of the parts, which
are variable among them, teaching the
art of joining, or constructing the ones with
the others, and finally giving rules for
proper and good pronunciation. Where-
fore, having to write a Grammar to
learn and teach the Mexican language,
it did not seem right to me to depart from the ordi-
nary path along which the Latin language
proceeds, which is better known among us,
nor did I want to oblige myself to follow
its rules entirely, because it would be to drag very
far from the purpose (and as they say) by
the hair many things that here require very
different precepts. So that in what-
ever I have been able to make use of Latin gram-
mar, I will always keep close to
it

Translation:

it; but of the other things, in which this language
differs from Latin, because they are new,
it has been necessary to reduce them to new
rules, with the new style that is required:
This grammar is therefore divided into five
books. In the first, it treats of the de-
clension of the noun. In the second, of the conjugation
of the verb. In the third, it teaches the order with
which some parts of speech are derived from
others. In the fourth book, instead of syn-
tax, or construction, because in this language there is no
such variation of cases, the art is set down
which they have in compounding some words with
others. The fifth and last book treats of the pro-
nunciation and accent, and even in this, hav-
ing availed ourselves of Latin in what
Mexican is similar to it, there are joint-
ly set down rules for the pronunciation and
new accents that are proper to this language,
and are not found in the others.

First Chapter, of the di-
versity and numbers of accents
that are found.

THE QUANTITY
of Mexican syllables
is of three kinds, because
there is a long syllable, and a short
syllable, and an equal syllable, which is neither long
nor short; long, e.g., atl, matl; short,
like tetl, cetl; equal, like tlaxcalli:
for that penult must neither be
lengthened nor shortened.

Thus, according to this diversity
of the quantity of the syllable, there are found
five

Translation:

[Header: Book five.]
five differences of accents, because
in the long syllable there is an acute and
grave accent. In the short syllable there is a
predominant short accent, and the saltillo. The syl-
lable of equal length has its similar accent
which is called a moderate accent. Acute
accent is that which, besides lengthening the
syllable, adds to it a tone that raises
the pronunciation with an acute sound,
e.g., milli, tlilli; grave accent is that which,
besides lengthening the syllable, adds a
grave sound with which it lowers the to-
ne, e.g., teotl, ciuatl; predominant short
accent is the one that by itself rules the
word where it is found with a pronunciation
accelerated and quick, e.g., mecatl, çacatl.
Accent of the saltillo is when the syl-
lable is pronounced with some
roughness, such as tlaçolli.
